刃 concerns a blade or cutting edge. The standalone word 刃 は names the cutting part of a knife or sword, not automatically the whole tool. The character also appears in words concerning swords.

Modern-shape mnemonic, not etymology: Compare 刀, "sword; blade," and notice the extra short inner mark, shaped like 丶. Let that mark remind you of the cutting edge. This is a memory aid for the modern shape, not a historical explanation.

This small lesson practices は. ジン, ニン and やいば remain recognition material here; leaving them out of practice does not make them invalid or uniformly rare. The source-only き.る is not a recommendation to replace the spelling of 切る きる, "cut," with an invented spelling.
刃 は — blade; cutting edge
刃物 はもの — edged tool; cutting instrument
刀 かたな names a sword; 刃 は can name its cutting part. Learn the whole word and context rather than treating the two characters as freely interchangeable.
乃, with connecting or particle-related uses, 凹, "concave; sunken," and 凸, "convex; protruding," do not share the blade/cutting-edge meaning.
The same spelling 刃 also has the reading やいば. Its dictionary senses are not all automatically senses of the noun は.

刃 は — blade; cutting edge
刃 is a noun naming the blade or cutting edge of a knife, sword or similar tool. This article teaches the reading は and the physical cutting-part sense.
この包丁の刃は鋭いです。 (このほうちょうのははするどいです。) — This kitchen knife's blade is sharp.
写真では、刃がよく見えます。 (しゃしんでは、はがよくみえます。) — The blade is clearly visible in the photograph.
In 包丁の刃 (ほうちょうのは), "the blade of a kitchen knife," の connects the tool with its cutting part. In 刃が見える (はがみえる), "the blade is visible," が marks what is visible.

刃 represents the whole native noun は here. There is no compound to split. The same written character also has the separate word reading やいば, "blade; sword"; that does not make every sense under やいば a sense of は.
ナイフ, "knife," and 包丁 ほうちょう, "kitchen knife," name whole tools. 刃 は focuses on the cutting part. Likewise, 刀 かたな and 日本刀 にほんとう name swords rather than just their cutting edges.
端 はし, "edge; end; tip," and 縁 ふち, "rim; edge," describe boundaries more broadly. Not every edge is a cutting edge. There is no single lexical antonym for 刃.

English "edge" can mean the edge of a desk or the boundary of an area. 刃 は does not generally replace 端 or 縁 for those spatial meanings. Learn it with a cutting tool and keep the distinction between the tool and its blade.
For figurative English "cutting edge" meaning the forefront of a field, use words such as 先端 せんたん, not 刃 は.
